question: An estimated 1-3 % of people in the world have coeliac disease. The only possible treatment and diet for those people is a gluten-free diet. Gluten-free products entail considerable extra costs, however. The Spanish Federation of Coeliac Associations’ 2025 price report shows that those extra costs can be more than EUR 1 000 per family every year.

Some Member States provide financial support or reimbursement to cover the cost of glutenfree food. Others, including Spain, however, provide little or no support, which makes it harder to acquire a basic necessity – food – and the treatment people with coeliac disease need. Given that the Commission has presented recommendations or guidelines in other areas of health: 1.
Is the Commission planning to study and compare support measures for people with coeliac disease in place in Member States?

Does the Commission believe it appropriate to include the issue in its forthcoming programmes to encourage Member States to take measures so people with coeliac disease have access to the specific food they need?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2025) The Gluten Free Regulation1 sets harmonised requirements for the labelling of foods as ‘gluten-free’ or ‘very-low gluten’. It applies to both prepacked and non-prepacked foods, such as those served in restaurants. These rules are based on scientific data and aim to prevent misleading and confusing the consumers from divergent food information.

In line with Article 168 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, the Commission complements national policies by providing support in reaching health policy objectives, through the framework initiative ‘Healthier Together’2, which addresses noncommunicable diseases.

The Expert Group on Public Health3, composed of national experts, assists and advises the Commission, including on the preparation of policy and legislative initiatives and activities addressing major public health challenges. It also organises exchange of best practices4, such as on effective actions to support coeliac patients.

The Commission continues to support the Member States through policy coordination and funding to encourage actions at national level on the management of conditions like coeliac disease. The implementation of measures on healthcare delivery and financial support to improve the access to specific foods for coeliac patients rests with the national authorities.

Finally, under the Horizon programmes, several projects5 have been funded to address gluten in food and personalised nutrition for individuals suffering from coeliac disease. Based on the results, new challenges could be addressed to identify possible gaps in research and innovation.
